Abstract

Four essays in, a value-content's whole history is on the table: which row of source it takes its standing from, through which place it became this person's, what happens structurally when the place is occupied, how it rises and falls in time. What is missing is what to do when two of them collide.

The object is value conflict: one person, two contents each already avowed, demanding incompatible actions in one concrete situation.

The whole essay has one line with different things on either side. On one side: constitution and standing — whether a row of source is present, whether a content has taken its standing in this person's own law, this person's standing as an end. Three things on that side, each its own, none interchangeable. On the other side: action — which content holds the centre of gravity now, whether new candidates can still surface on each row, whether contents are added or lost. The conflict is entirely on the second side, and so is the adjudication. And the action side does not settle across into the first: relational acts can seal the road to that side, and can make a reading that looks like constitution, and cannot perform constituting. If anything on the first side changed, this person did something else over there.

What most needs guarding against here is not saying too little. It is handing over a ruler. Conflict pushes the question of an order of action right up in front of you, and once an order gets its grounds written down the grounds get read as gradations: the reader lays the grounds out as a weighting table and asks which scores higher. The head proposition of this series is it has structure, and admits no ranking, and practical situations do not stop producing orders of action and outcomes on that account. Fail to cut the two apart and this essay reads either as in a conflict you may decline to choose, or as the series has finally admitted that values rank.

The line to hold was printed long ago: unranked in being does not mean practical situations produce no order of action. And only the order formed by the bearer's own law is what this essay calls adjudication. It is an order in action, not a ranking of value-standing.

1. One Afternoon

A man has two things he set for himself: a book he has been writing for years, and a craft he opened up on his own. Both come out of the 14DD row — one's own ends and their flourishing. This afternoon is enough for one of them.

That is the case this essay handles: under one bearer, two contents each already avowed, demanding incompatible actions in one concrete situation. Incompatible is said of the actions, not of the contents. Both contents are there, both are his, and only one can be done this afternoon.

Several situations look the same from outside. One: a man has stopped doing that thing the old way lately. It looks as if it collided with something, and in fact that content is changing on its own. The two cuts fall here — first, was there a first-person constituting act in this change; if not, it is a rise or fall in running; if so, has the original claiming terminated: not terminated is revision, terminated is withdrawal. In the revision cell there is only ever one content, and no two things holding against each other.

Another: today he suddenly wants very much to go home early, and the work on his desk is not finished. The line is not whether going home early looks like a preference. A preference can be a candidate content's first appearance, and it can equally be an established value-content expressing itself in present action — a man who has long cherished caring for his family therefore chooses to come home early today. Preference does not lock to one layer, and a present preference is not enough to establish that a content already is value-content, nor that it is not. So if wanting to go home early is only wanting it now, it is not this case; if it is the present expression of an avowed value, then two values really are colliding.

A third: two people each holding one thing, at odds. That is not a matter of two contents under one bearer; its structure is elsewhere, and the last sections take it up.

Two more things have to hold. The two contents must belong to one bearer. And that bearer's first-person ordering of action must already be able to run in this content-domain. Subjects-to-be, and people who have temporarily lost that running, fall on the boundary; not unfolding them here is not a judgment that they have no value.

Two contents belonging to one person does not mean no one else is in the situation. Belonging says whose each content is; it says nothing about who else is around this afternoon.

2. Standing Admits Only Holding or Not

That afternoon he will ask himself: which one matters more.

To say a content has standing is to ask one thing only: has it taken, in the bearer's own law, the standing avowal confers. First-person avowal is a constituting event by which a candidate content takes a first-person status of being invocable, restatable and revisable, and that place can be neither granted nor revoked from outside. There is no quantity in the definition. As regards the standing avowal confers, a content has either taken it or not yet; there is no third case, and the two here fall in the first. The predicate has no taken it a bit more or a bit less. Higher, lower, equal — comparisons of that kind are not in this predicate's domain of definition.

A person's identification with a value can be ambiguous, can waver, can take years to settle. Why insist it is only holding or not.

Wavering, strength, attention and the centre of gravity each have their own subject, and all are readings on the running side; standing is not the same thing. By degrees describes the process of entering that standing: some avowals occur in a moment, some take shape by degrees and settle only after years, and calling it a constituting event says what it completes structurally, not that it must fall on a single point in time. What is being weighed here is two contents whose claiming is already complete; and once the question is whether this content has become his value-content, the predicate takes only holding or not. Not one of the real ambiguities of experience has been deleted. They simply do not fall on standing.

3. Conflict Falls on Joint Realizability

Standing answers whether this one is his, and the answer is only holding or not. Whether the two things they demand right now can both be done is another question.

Conflict is that second question answered no: jointly unrealizable. And joint realizability is a property of demands for action, not a property of standing. This content is his, and that content is also his, and between those two sentences there is nothing that could get in the other's way, because holding and holding do not collide. What collides is that there is only one afternoon.

So conflict does not fall on the side of standing. The reason is not that there is no ruler over there. Even if there were, two gradations would not become incompatible by sitting on one table. The reason is that there is nothing over there that could be jointly realized.

And if no revision or withdrawal separately occurs, the two contents' existing standing yields no higher and lower, cannot declare either void, and certainly cannot compute out of both are my values which one to do this afternoon.

That book and that craft come out of the same 14DD row. Even for someone who still thinks the four rows rank, there are no two comparable items here: same row, same bearer, both avowed. And the conflict is real, and this afternoon is real, and the question of an order of action is still standing right in front of him.

The thing he is asking after does not exist in the place he is asking. He still has to sit down at two o'clock and do one of them.

4. The Sense of Higher and Lower

Sitting in that afternoon, it is hard not to wonder which one is more important. The thought does not come from nowhere. It really is reading something. What it reads is just not where it thinks it is.

The four rows do make more dimensions available as the DD levels rise. A bearer unfolded to 15DD does not have the same number of dimensions to hand as one unfolded only to 12DD. That layer is structural, and it falls on the history of construction and on available dimensions. Richness came with three limits attached, one of which is that there is no quantity on the value-standing side. More and fewer say what one can use, not what one is worth.

The direction of going up is real too as a condition. A person can stop at the rows of source he has and lose nothing by not taking up more; and what the structure now standing has not exhausted keeps giving a legitimate bridge that can be taken up. A bridge gives a condition on direction. It does not perform the uptake for the bearer. So the structure gives only the direction one may open toward. It does not adjudicate which of two existing rows is lighter.

There is one more asymmetry, and it appears only at sources later in the structural order. When such a source has conditions of application that have actually arisen, and the bearer actively closes that source's running, that does not count as neutral going-back. What is closed is the running, not the fact that the source-position was once gained. This asymmetry does not say the later one is worth more. It says the source's conditions of application are present now and the bearer shut it off. No direction-value attribution was assigned to that either.

One more thing gets read as ranking by structural order: the window for action. A book not written today can still be written tomorrow; a person not visited today may not be here tomorrow. What is being separated here is whether deferring closes off the same opportunity — not whether an action, once begun, can be taken back. Those are two questions. The window is something he really will look at. What is misread is the correlation between it and the structural order.

And the correlation reverses. For a man near starving, the demand on the lowest row has the tightest window of all, and the damage of missing it is the least reversible: the life ends and nothing else need be discussed. If an order of action really could be read straight off the structural order, this is the counter-example; and if one says instead that lower always takes priority, ordinary afternoons are the counter-example. Both readings turn a situation's window and damage into gradations of value-standing. That the correlation reverses is itself the proof that it is not structure.

So someone steps back and says: then the ranking of values varies with the situation. That step invites the ruler back in, with a parameter added. What varies with the situation is the order of action, not value-standing. The order of action was never a ranking of value in the first place, so its varying says nothing about anything changing over on the standing side. A man writes first yesterday and works the craft first today, and across those two days not one content's standing moved by a hair.

5. Yielding Is Not Withdrawal

That afternoon he did one and not the other. Where the undone one stands in his own law depends only on whether a revision or withdrawal separately occurred. Not on the not-doing.

An order of action, the results of carrying it out, and what others do to him cannot by themselves rewrite a content's value-standing. Claiming, revision and withdrawal are structurally permanent: relational things can seal the road to them and cannot take them away. The most constitution-like thing the outside can produce is still only a reading — attribution belongs on the side of social recognition, which has no constituting power, so nothing is constituted there, only a reading taken as constitution. And a bearer's own closing of a source later in the structural order changes that row's reachability, not its presence; the history of construction cannot be erased, and what is shut off is the running.

So yielding is not withdrawal. Not because he restrained himself from withdrawing, but because the act of yielding simply cannot do what withdrawal does. Yielding is on the side of the order of action; withdrawal is on the side of constitution. They are not on the same side. He did not write the book today, and that fact by itself cannot move where the book stands in his own law.

If a content's standing really did change, then another first-person revision or withdrawal occurred. The change comes from that constituting act, not from the yielding.

That governs the act of yielding itself. What becomes of the yielded content afterwards has to be asked separately, and there are four different questions with four different subjects. Their answers can differ pairwise: the content is still avowed while today's demand no longer holds; the window has closed while that row still throws up new candidates. Rolling them into one state and asking how is the yielded one doing now asks after nothing real.

The questionIts subjectWhat answers it
Is it still avowed by himvalue-standingOnly revision or withdrawal changes it. Not the passage of time, not attention moving away
Does today's demand for action still holdthe situationVaries with the situation. The child grew up, the appointment lapsed — the demand may cease while the content stays his
Is the window for that same action still openthe actionSome windows do not reopen; some come round next year. This is on the action side, and is not called reachability
Can new candidates still surface on that rowthe row of sourceReachability proper, read per row of source, out of his own working

6. Adjudication Is Judged Apart from Constitution

An adjudication is itself an arrangement on the order of action. Whether a constituting act also occurred during a conflict is not answered by whether the thing was an adjudication. It is answered by the two cuts: was there a first-person constituting act, and has the original claiming terminated.

A person really can settle a conflict by way of revision or withdrawal. He worked it out that afternoon: the craft he no longer holds as his own thing, and takes it up from now on only as a pastime. That is a withdrawal, and it is real — and it was not accomplished by the adjudication. Both can happen inside one stretch of deciding, and each still settles by its own subject.

And when two avowed contents collide, what actually gets done can still be organized by something else. Someone was on the phone pressing him and he went; his hand moved first and habit chose for him; he was too tired and picked one at random; or he followed a set of practices picked up elsewhere that has never taken standing in his own law. All of these can close this afternoon's window, and none of them is what this essay calls adjudication.

What enters first-person practical adjudication is an order of action formed by the bearer's own law, with two avowed contents as the two ends of the conflict. This is the same restriction the centre of gravity carries, and it holds down the other end at the same time: no reading does not mean low value, and does not mean the action does not count.

The concrete relations, the boundaries, what damage would be done, which one can be deferred — all of these can enter as grounds of adjudication, and none of them has first to become a value-content of his. That the child is now unattended is a fact about a relation; that this damage cannot be made up afterwards is a judgment about consequences. Both can change how he orders this afternoon, and neither needs to have been avowed as a value first.

Since adjudication has to hold within his own law, does his final choice therefore reveal which one really belongs to him? The inference fails, and the reason is structural: adjudication takes the existing avowals as its premise, and therefore cannot turn round and certify them.

At most it shows which avowed contents actually organized the order in that one action. It cannot prove those avowals were not colonized, and it cannot say which of them is more truly his own. That layer was sealed when self-colonization was raised: audit reads only whether the places are open or shut and does not judge what the bearer really avows; an audit that reaches past those three generates, structurally, exactly the relation introjection requires. And what is missing there was never permission at the level of type — it is discovery. Nor can that judgment be contemporaneous: taken as contains within it that one has not, at this moment, seen it to be external, and a man who sees in the moment that this is not from under his own sources dissolves the taking-as on the spot.

So what that afternoon leaves is material he can look back on later. Not a procedure that determines anything on the spot.

7. The Conflict Takes No Direction-Reading of Itself

Direction-value appraises a transformation, and both its directions require two subjects: an enactment loosening the other's grid and opening new dimensions, or sealing the other's grid and cutting available dimensions away. Two contents under one person holding against each other have, as the two ends of that holding, not two subjects. So the conflict itself takes no direction-reading. It is neither benign nor malign; that column is undefined for it.

The concrete action the conflict produces is another matter. He fired the kiln this afternoon and it burned all night, and the neighbour did not sleep. That action landed on someone else, and whether it cut anything away is read by the power-theory criterion; this essay does not read it for them. The conflict takes no direction-reading and the action the conflict produces takes no direction-reading are two sentences, and only the first holds.

After that afternoon is over, do not roll several things into one question. Adjudication gives only the present order of action. Whether new candidates surface on each row afterwards, whether contents are added or lost, does not settle out of the adjudication itself; to change, it has to be traced separately to which thing he actually did, how he did it, what happened in the world afterwards, or to some later running event.

If no revision or withdrawal separately occurred, nothing on the side of constitution and standing moved because of this afternoon: the rows of source he has gained are still present, the book and the craft stand where they stood in his own law, and his standing as an end has nothing to do with this afternoon.

The adjudication, the thing he actually chose, his carrying it through, and the consequences it left in the world are four things. Each has its own time, its own subject, its own settling. Rolling them together as what the adjudication changed presses four things into one.

8. Five Grounds, and the Gap

The two contents' existing standing does not yield which one to do this afternoon. He does not therefore sit there doing nothing. He is looking at other things.

He looks at who is present in this afternoon and what relations he stands in with them. He looks at what this next move touches in whom, and where that boundary gets brushed — and how that boundary is contested, and by what procedure disputes over it are handled, belongs to rights theory. He looks at what damage cannot be made up afterwards: the subject here is the damage, not his decision and not whether he can change his mind later. He looks at whether going ahead can still be taken back — that is revocability, whose subject is the action. And he looks at what becomes of the one he yields, which is the four questions above, each running by its own domain of definition and not rolled into one.

The window sits inside those four questions, and it is not the same question as revocability: a thing can be done in a way that stays changeable throughout, while the window is only today.

These five share no common scale, carry no weights, and cannot be laid out as one table. Each asks a different thing, and what each turns up cannot be converted into the others.

They do have local priorities of domain — not a chain running end to end. You have to know who is present, and what this move touches in whom, before the corresponding relations and boundaries can be unfolded, and before it can be read whose the damage is. Whether it can be taken back is judged by the action itself, and does not need to wait on who is present. The yielded one is the same: where it stands in his own law depends only on whether a revision or withdrawal separately occurred; that row's reachability is a reading of his own working; whether the demand still holds and whether the window is still open each follow their own situation.

There is a structure of diagnosis. There is no procedure that walks from the first to the fifth, and there is certainly no algorithm of adjudication.

9. No Rule Closes the Gap

He will think: perhaps I should set myself a rule — when in doubt, take the one that can still be undone.

Theory can of course propose such candidates. It cannot exempt that rule from the step its application to this one afternoon requires. Set up a condition for applying the conditions, and that one has itself to be applied to the case; the gap has only moved to the next line of the list, and a list does not close by getting longer. Whether the rule is one of his own law is a separate question. The gap is not there waiting for a stronger cause to fill it. It is where this structure is simply open. The bearer stands there.

Where a rule comes from, and by what it binds him, are two questions. A rule's content can come from a teacher, from a tradition, from a book; provenance does not judge whether it is an alien ruler — provenance was taken out of the judgment when colonization was raised. Whether it is a line of his own law settles separately.

Those five are themselves conditions. Complete, they still do not entail which one he does this afternoon.

As for irreversibility, it does not get a line of its own, because it has no single subject. Damage may not be made up; an action may not be taken back; the yielded one may meet a window that never reopens. The three stay in the third, fourth and fifth grounds respectively, each asking its own can this be recovered, and they do not combine into one aggregate weight of irreversibility. By the two-axes rule, it does not read back into value-standing either.

What prudence there is to be had about this afternoon's action belongs to the theory of action. Whether these things ought to be so belongs to the second critique.

10. The Man Next Door

The neighbour comes over. He also has a thing of his own that he has been at for years, and it needs him up before dawn — and once the kiln is lit it burns all night. Two people, each with something he set for himself, and only one of them can happen tonight.

The two of them can sit down and settle something: the kiln moves to those few days mid-month, and on those days he gets up late. That decision is real, and it really does bind both sides.

It has not thereby produced a third party ranking each man's values for him. Why he is bound by that decision settles separately — by consent, by promise, by the moral law, by rights and institutions — and those settlings are not this essay's business. What is denied here is one thing only: two people settling something does not mean two sets of values have been merged into one common table, and does not mean a place has appeared from which either side's order can be set.

Settling something did not generate that place, and saying so does not require first exhausting every possible place. What the decision binds here is the arrangement of action the two agreed on and the responsibilities that follow. It has not thereby acquired authority to rank either side's value-standing. If some collective subject can be established, it has to prove that by its own conditions of constitution, and cannot be inferred from this one joint decision.

What the two of them settled is this: each one's value-belongings unchanged, and the arrangement of action landing in one place.

11. A Settlement Cannot Complete Anyone's Withdrawal

Suppose the neighbour's condition is: from now on, stop holding that craft as your own thing.

The demand can be made, and it may genuinely make a person think it over again. But whether a claiming has terminated can be completed only by that person's own withdrawal. First-person avowal cannot be granted by another and cannot be revoked by another. The outside can do a great deal — it can suppress expression, block reachability, make life unliveable — and not one of those completes a revocation in the modality of avowal.

The judgment here goes in three steps. Is this only an external requirement? Has it sealed his revision and expression, blocked the road to those places? Has it gone further and registered an external end as his own value? Only with the third does it settle under colonization. If the first is only a requirement, it stays only a requirement. If the second has further sealed the road to revision, expression or running, that falls to coercion, to a violation of rights, to a blocking in running — rights theory and power theory. Only the third reaches the colonization of value.

A settlement can produce severe suppression or a violation of rights and still not be the colonization of value. The two do not combine into one.

Two orders of action, each formed on its own, meeting in this one night is not a joint adjudication ranking both sides' value-standing. It is two orders landing in one arrangement. What can be arranged where they meet is each side's actions — how resources are staggered, who moves the thing that is in the way. The outside can also supply supporting conditions: time, materials, a steadier situation. It cannot arrange what candidates will surface on the other's rows of source; that is sustained by his own working, and still less can it stand in for his constituting.

The other is an end, and from this it follows that he too has his own ends and values was established long ago. Tonight it has a place where it actually bears — and a place where it bears is not a place where it is grounded: one may not turn it round and say because I see he has values of his own, he is an end.

Nor can one say the two sides' values are equally important. Equally is still two gradations on one ruler. What has to be said is something else: the place that thing occupies in him, and the place this thing occupies in me, are positions of the same type in their respective structures — and they do not constitute a common quantity.

12. What Remains

Conflict falls on whether two demands for action can both be met, not on the two contents' standing. Adjudication arranges only this afternoon's order of action; later changes in reachability and in contents do not settle out of the adjudication itself, and have to be traced separately to what he chose, to the carrying out, to the consequences, or to later running events — and none of those reads back into value-standing.

Yielding is not withdrawal, because the act of yielding cannot do what withdrawal does. If a standing really changed, another first-person revision or withdrawal occurred. A joint decision does not thereby generate a third place of value adjudication; what two people settle is that each one's value-belongings are unchanged and the arrangement of action lands in one place.

How the one still his, and yielded this afternoon, goes on being borne by the same life belongs to the theory of meaning.

How an order of action is formed, carried out, and looked back on, and how judgment, habit, hesitation and capacity enter it, belongs entirely to the theory of action. This essay does not use them and passes no verdict on them.

Why another's value cannot be exhaustively read, cannot be compared by a common outside ruler, cannot be unified into one set, and how resonance between two bearers happens, belongs to the essay on the other.
prequel:
Abstract

The word value is claimed at once by the market, by ethics, and by ordinary speech. One word carries at least three different things, so before it can be let into the framework the space it refers to has to be cleared.

The clearing is not done by arguing with anyone. It is done by showing, for each of five common misidentifications, the level or the category at which it sits askew: price, direction, a price set on the remainder, a ladder, and each-to-their-own. The essay carries one instrument with a positive shape — the solitary subject. The lowest condition for end-value to stand asks for no counterparty; price asks for at least two subjects and a common measure. Once the conditions under which two things exist part ways over the count of subjects, they are not two readings of one thing. They are two things.

The emblem of the series is an old story about a pearl and a casket. The five sections that follow clear, in fact, five caskets.

1. The Pearl and the Casket

There is an old story. A seller of pearls set a pearl into a casket wrought with the utmost craft — the wood precious, scented, inlaid with jade. The buyer paid, kept the casket, and returned the pearl.

Later ages laughed at that buyer. This series takes the story for its emblem, but what it takes is not the laughter.

The buyer had a ready ruler to hand. The worth of the wood, the strength of the scent, the fineness of the carving, the density of the inlay — all of it comparable, priceable, exchangeable. He could measure the casket.

The pearl was not on that ruler.

He did not fail to see the pearl. His ruler could not measure it, and so the thing it could not measure was returned as nothing.

The error of keeping the casket and returning the pearl is not in buying the casket. The casket truly has its craft, its price, its market. The error is in taking the priceable half for the whole of value and returning the half that cannot be priced. His problem was not that he bought a casket. It was that all he had in hand was a casket's ruler.

The five sections below clear five caskets.

2. The First Casket: Price

Price is the most common and the most forceful misreading of value.

The force is earned. Of all the ways of speaking about value, price is the one most open to operation: it can be measured, compared, entered in a ledger, forecast. A measurable reading expands of its own accord into the immeasurable, and so what is this worth is heard, in ordinary speech, almost always as what does this cost. The more a market succeeds, the more this hearing looks like the only one.

This section does not deny that price is real. It only moves price out of the answer-place of what value is.

First a boundary of usage. By price is meant the market reading of exchange, conversion, and common measure. A solitary person can still weigh two of their own uses against each other, reckon the cost of a trade-off, set scarcity in an order of precedence — those are their own reckonings, and they are not price. Price asks for more than a calculation. It asks for a counterparty.

Consider where each thing that makes price price actually happens. Exchange asks for a ceding end and a receiving end. Comparison asks for a common measure, and a measure becomes common only when at least two subjects grant it. Conversion, summation, quotation, bargaining — every one of these motions presupposes a market, and a market is at fewest two subjects. What price reads is not a thing in itself but the position of a thing within a many-subject structure of exchange.

Now lower the count of subjects to one.

Imagine the first and only subject in a universe. It has no second end to exchange with, no second subject to grant a shared measure. Price on it is not equal to zero — it has no domain of definition. The function price takes no value on a single subject.

And value stays whole. That solitary subject still lives inside the difference between good and bad, still keeps to its own bounds, still sets its own ends. It has its own value, and it has no price of its own.

This is no figure of speech but a parting of the conditions of existence. For value to stand asks for one subject and its own law. For price to stand asks for at least two subjects and a common measure. Once the conditions under which two concepts exist part ways over the count of subjects, they are not two readings of one thing but two things.

Once parted, each side keeps its place. Price is not thereby made false: the market is a real structure, price is a real reading, there is a real loss when end-value is coded into price, and measuring that loss is the work of the Economics papers. And value is not thereby made mysterious: it simply does not stand within the domain of price.

Two directions of overreach are the only things to guard against. In one, price swallows value: whatever cannot be priced is without value — and then the universe of the solitary subject becomes a universe without value, a conclusion enough to bring the path down. In the other, value swallows price: the market reading is judged a fallen form of value, and trade a profanation of ends. Neither is taken here.

3. The Second Casket: Direction

Power Theory set down a line: value lies in the direction and not in the remainder.

That line is true within Power Theory. But the value in it means direction-value, which is a distinct sense from this series' end-value. Two senses sharing one word is the second most common source of misreading in the discussion of value.

Direction-value is an orientation-reading of a single transformation. An exercise that loosens the other's lattice, opening new dimensions with no old source demeaned, is cultivation. An exercise that locks the other's lattice, cutting away workable dimensions, is severing.

What matters is this: direction-value appraises the transformation itself, whether it opens dimension or closes it. It does not appraise the subjects at either end, does not appraise their value-sources, and least of all ranks the two ends. Good and ill fall to the account of the transformation, not to the account of persons.

Mix the two senses and a class of sentences appears at once. The cultivated one's value has risen and the severed one's has fallen; whoever cultivates is worth more than whoever severs; a person inside a relation full of cultivation is worth more than a person inside a relation full of severing.

Such sentences enter the reading of a transformation into the account of subject-standing. The error is one of category: the domain of direction-value is transformations, the domain of end-value is subjects. A transformation may be judged benign or ill, and the standing of the subjects at either end, as ends, is not increased or decreased by a hair. The severed person's situation has worsened and their workable dimensions have thinned — those are real losses. But their value as an end has not been marked down.

And there is a turn here worth pausing on. It is precisely because end-value is not marked down by severing that severing is the kind of thing that has to be judged ill. If severing really could reduce the other's value, then severing would be a repricing — and repricing belongs to the sense cut away in the section before.

4. The Third Casket: A Price on the Remainder

Power Theory set down that the remainder has no price. Rights Theory set a lock in the same place: to imagine the remainder as a treasure hidden at the innermost layer, once the dimensions are peeled away, is to misread a dynamic operational term as a pearl.

This series takes the pearl as its marker precisely in order to tighten that lock, not to loosen it.

Setting a price on the remainder commits two errors in one motion.

The first is substantialization. The remainder is not a possessable thing. Whoever cups it as a treasure has already made a specimen of a dynamic operational term.

The second is pricing. The motion of pricing belongs to the first casket — all pricing presupposes a common measure and a market, and the remainder is exactly the place no measure exhausts.

The two errors often conspire into a third saying: the remainder has no price, therefore the remainder's price is infinitely high.

That saying sounds like elevation and is in fact demolition. An infinitely high price is still a price, still inside the domain of pricing, still waiting for a large enough bid to redeem it. Pricelessness is not the maximum of price. It is being outside the domain of pricing. To render the unpriceable as beyond all price is the most common way this kind of talk pulls its own house down.

5. The Fourth Casket: The Ladder

Value-sources differ with a subject's structural level — that is the figure this series will raise on the positive side. But differ with level is most easily heard as rise with level.

As though there were a ladder of value: the lower levels' sources are elementary value, the higher levels' are advanced value, the subject climbs, value mounts rung by rung, and the top rung caps it. There is a popular figure that draws needs as a pyramid, subsistence at the base and self-realization at the peak, the life at the apex worth more than the life at the bottom.

That figure has to come down.

The ladder confuses two orders. What a level gives is a position of generation: which structure appears first and which after. This order is real, an order of construction, and it is not denied. What it does not give is a rank of value.

A subject that unfolds a new level has only gained workable structural dimensions. It is not thereby worth more than its earlier self, and still less worth more than another subject who has stayed at the earlier level. A new level's source is an addition, not a replacement — the higher level keeps and re-places the lower sources, and no level's source is voided or marked down in the ascent.

The ladder has a more hidden version, too: it ranks not levels but directions. It grants that each level's sources are true in their own right, and then says that upward movement itself proves the upper worth more, that the existence of a direction is the existence of a rank.

Half of that version was already cut in the section before: the reading of a direction appraises the transformation, not the two ends. A dimension-opening exercise judged benign does not make the end it opens onto worth more.

6. The Fifth Casket: Each to Their Own

Take the ladder down and the nearest pit is in the reverse direction.

If there is no rank of value, no outside measure standing over all subjects, then is not anything one says as good as anything else? Every one a measure, all measures equal, value become each-to-their-own, whatever a subject declares valuable at this moment being valuable by that declaration.

This reading hears unranked as unstructured, and the two are a whole series apart.

What was deleted is only the outside lateral measure — that ruler standing over the law of every subject, by which subjects might be ranked against one another. To delete this ruler is to delete the instrument of ranking, not the structure itself.

Not one piece of structure was deleted. A value-source is not something a subject declares offhand; it is given with the subject's structural level. What a subject happens to like at this moment is a particular preference. A preference can be wrong, can change, can be hijacked; it does not by that fact become the subject's value-source. To equate preference straightway with value is the first step down the each-to-their-own path, and the easiest door for an outside end to walk through.

Beyond structure, each-to-their-own misses a second thing: it reads the inner as an island. Since value is each subject's own, between subjects there is only talking to oneself.

One's own law has already furnished the counter-example. Every subject's law is laid down by that subject itself, and no one can exhaustively read or write another's law — yet law and law recognize each other in form, the same internal double-negation recurring in every self-legislating subject.

Value is isomorphic with law. Each subject's value-source is given out of its own structure, and precisely because the same structure recurs from subject to subject, the values each gives out can resonate.

Resonance is not a common measure: a measure ranks, resonance recognizes. When two subjects, each giving out its own value from its own law, meet, they need no shared ruler to translate.

But isomorphism yields only the possibility of recognition. It does not guarantee that the content is the same, nor that recognition in fact occurs. And resonance is not a condition for value to stand: a value with which no one resonates is not for that reason demoted — the first casket's criterion holds the floor here, for what resonates is already whole in the solitary subject.

There is a fine but load-bearing distinction here: resonance only occurs with the arrival of a second subject, whereas price is constituted by the second subject. The one is a trigger, the other a constitution. That is the line between resonance and price.

So the governing proposition of this series is a line that bites at both ends: it has structure, and admits no ranking.

Against the ladder it says: no ranking. Against each-to-their-own it says: it has structure. Each error holds one end, and the proposition stands in the middle.

And the cost of admitting no ranking is not the loss of structure — it is those two paths themselves that lose structure. The ladder trades away the true sources of the levels for a false ruler. Each-to-their-own, in the pose of abolishing all rulers, abolishes the difference between source and preference, and miscounts the resonance between subjects as impossible. Neither price is paid here.

7. The Useless Is Not the Worthless

There is an old strand of teaching that seats the highest place in the useless: what enters no use is thereby preserved whole. The use of the useless is the great use.

This strand collides, on the surface, with the ground of this series. The root of the series is self as an end — to set up an end on one hand and exalt the non-end on the other looks like working at cross purposes.

Take them apart and there is no collision.

Useless says: not used up as a means — not conscripted to the end by any purpose-loop, not exhausted by any inventory of uses. Self as an end says: not reduced — the subject not degraded to a bare means.

The two are not one proposition. They meet only on the one face of anti-instrumentalization, the one speaking from not exhausted by another's uses, the other from itself being an end.

For a bearer, to keep from being used up as a means is exactly to keep the place of an end. A bearer may enter another's purpose-loop, may help others get things done, may take on a role of office or of care, and still not forfeit its place as an end — so long as it has not been reduced to a bare means, and its first-person positions of avowal, revision, and exit have not been cancelled.

The divide is not in whether one is of use to another, but in whether that use issues from one's own law. Devotion runs from within outward, one's own end unfolding toward the world. A subject that trades of its own motion has its own end taking the market as a tool, and price has not climbed into the site where its value comes to be. Both of these are still one's own end.

What is reduced to a bare means is another case: an outside inventory of uses has written one's value in one's stead.

A subject that takes another's inventory of uses to avow its own value has already had the site of its value's occurrence occupied by that inventory, so that thereafter, looking at itself, it sees first only a usable self. The use of the useless keeps exactly this site from being moved into — readings of use may come and go, and who gives the value does not change hands.

But this strand carries a slope of its own, to be locked here in the same breath: erecting the useless itself as a higher value, as though the less useful were the nobler, use vulgar and uselessness refined.

That is again to erect a ruler. The ladder the fourth casket took down is set back up facing the other way, the apex changing occupants, the tower the same tower.

This series takes the single sense of keeping-the-place: the use of the useless keeps the place of an end; it is not a ranking of uselessness.

8. Two Locks

The emblem takes two locks. Without them the emblem would itself become a sixth casket.

The first: the pearl is a structural place, not a substance.

The pearl means end-value, the standing of a subject as an end. It is not a treasure inside the subject's body. Rights Theory's lock bears repeating in this very place: to misread a dynamic operational term as a pearl is the error of substantialization.

That this series dares take the pearl for its marker rests precisely on setting this lock first upon the marker itself.

The second: pearl and casket divide only reference, not rank.

The casket has its structural function and its legitimacy. The market is a real structure, price a real reading, the craftsman's skill a real skill. The motion of this series is to tell pearl from casket, not to discard the casket and seize the pearl.

Once more, then, on the buyer's error: it was not that he bought the casket; it was that all he had in hand was a casket's ruler.

Return finally to the solitary subject and look at the pair of emblems once more. There is no market there, no buying and selling, no going rate for boxes — the casket has no object. The pearl is there still: that one subject is an end just the same, and has its own value just the same.

The casket arrives with the second subject. The pearl arrives with no one. It was already there.

9. The Table of Three Senses

With the five caskets cleared, the space to which the word value refers inside the framework can be gathered into a table.

SenseWhat it refers toCondition of existenceWhere it belongs
PriceThe market reading of exchange and comparisonAt least two subjects and a common measureSAE Economics
Direction-valueThe orientation-reading of a transformation (cultivation / severing)A relation of exercise between subjectsPower Theory
End-valueA bearer's standing as an end; one's own valueOne bearer, no counterparty requiredValue Theory

Each of the three senses is true, each has its domain, each has where it belongs. Confuse any two and you fall back into one of the caskets.

The sole object of this series is the third row.

10. After the Clearing

The prequel's work ends here.

What it has not done should be said plainly. It has built no positive machinery. Who bears end-value, how sources are given with level, how the value axis and the dynamic axis stand side by side without trespassing — none of that is here. Not one numbered proposition has been set.

It has only cleared the space to which the word value refers, and drawn the boundary of that space with the closing table.

But a clearing cannot be carried out in a complete positive vacuum. So it has borrowed three minimal boundary commitments: that end-value does not take a relation of exchange as its source; that value-standing is not ranked by any common outside measure; and that a particular preference is not by that fact a source of value. The burden of proving all three rests with what follows. Where the island-reading was refuted, one further minimal positive shape was borrowed — resonance — whose full portrait is also held for later.

The rest is the work of the papers to come: how value appears, how it is avowed in the first person, how it is socially recognized; how an outside end takes the site, is introjected, locks in; how value stabilizes, decays, shifts, recurs; how action is adjudicated when incommensurable structures of value meet; and why another's value cannot be exhaustively read, cannot be compared by an outside measure, cannot be merged — and how resonance happens exactly within those three limits.

The space of reference is cleared. The stakes are left for the papers that follow to drive.

Abstract

The previous essay raised the source. A source is a synchronic fact: it says which classes of content are able to land in a bearer, not which ones have landed. This essay is about what happens in time.

The head structure is a geometry. One axis of occurrence, crossed by one axis of recognition. On the axis of occurrence there are two places — appearance, which puts a content into candidacy, and first-person avowal, which is the sole constituting place. Social recognition is not a third rung. It is a second axis crossing the first: real, consequential, able to give a public place and to take it back, unable only to claim anything on your behalf.

Then the modal asymmetry that makes auditing possible: appearance is plastic, avowal is constitutive and cannot be granted or revoked from outside, recognition is grantable and revocable and constitutes nothing. Then shaping — what outside action can legitimately do to the conditions of occurrence — and its two forms, cultivation and evocation. Whichever form it takes, the last step stays with the bearer.

1. A Source Gives the Slot; Occurrence Fills It

Say of someone that he has the row of source that runs toward others. You have said something structural, and you have said nothing whatever about his afternoon. You do not know whom he cares for. You do not know whether he has yet met anyone at all.

A value-source is a synchronic structural ground, given with the bearer's structure. The occurrence of value is the process, in time, by which a class of concrete content comes to be that bearer's value-content. It has a before and an after, it has steps, it can be completed, and it can stop halfway.

A bearer that has just unfolded the row of source oriented toward others may not yet have met any particular other, and so nothing has yet occurred on that row. The source is there; occurrence has not begun. That is not a defect. It is two things belonging to two levels.

The first consequence of the two levels is that they are stable to different degrees. Within the range where the bearer's structure still stands, the presence of a source is given by structure and does not vanish because one concrete content has vanished. Concrete contents, by contrast, arise and pass: a content can occur, can decay, can be suppressed, can surface again. Fuse the two and you get an absurd inference — a man's particular devotion fades, and therefore that entire row of his value-source is gone.

The second consequence is that they give different things. The source gives a structural possibility: which class of content can enter this bearer's field of end-value. Occurrence makes good on this particular one. The source is the slot; occurrence is the filling of it. An empty slot is still a slot.

Decoupled is not severed. Occurrence always runs inside what the source makes possible. Without the corresponding row of source, that class of content has nowhere to land. The source gives the range; occurrence lands inside it.

And occurrence does not presuppose any dimension-opening. The vast majority of concrete contents occur within source-domains the bearer already has, and involve no new structural dimension at all.

2. One Axis of Occurrence, One Axis of Recognition

Three layers is the most natural thing to say here, and it is wrong. Three layers suggests three homogeneous steps in order, with nothing finished until the third has been taken.

Appearance and first-person avowal are two places on one axis. Appearance sends a content into candidacy; avowal makes it the bearer's own value-content. At avowal the occurrence is complete. From then on, though no one knows of it and no one grants it anything, it is already this bearer's value-content.

Social recognition does not add a station to that axis. It belongs to another one. It changes where this content stands in a field of many subjects — seen or unseen, sayable or unsayable, supported or blocked. It does not change whether the content is this bearer's value.

The geometry is one axis of occurrence plus one axis of recognition. Not three rungs of a ladder.

Nor can the three be reduced to one another. A content showing up in your view, and that content becoming yours, are two things. Avowal is not seeing it more clearly; it is a constituting event. Another holding this content to be valuable, or holding this content to be your value, is not you having avowed it. And the converse holds as well: a man may settle something for himself and gain thereby no place at all in which to say it.

Once the three are apart, a content's state in a given bearer can be read exactly. Let A stand for appearance, F for first-person avowal, S for social recognition.

The S in the table differs by its object. In the rows without F, S can only be content-recognition — the community holds this class of content to be valuable. Subject-place recognition, the community's holding that this content is a value this bearer has claimed, is not yet defined before F, since it presupposes a first-person place already there.

Four things are read off the table. F is the constituting place: only at F does a content become the bearer's value-content. A runs in the modality of plasticity, not of grant and revocation — the outside can present, block or suppress, so that a content shows up in the candidate field, or disappears, or becomes hard to enter. That is causal action on the conditions of appearing, not some relational subject granting or withdrawing candidacy. Grantable-and-revocable, as a relational modality, lands only on S.

A plus S does not impersonate F. A content pushed in front of you and held valuable by the community is still not your value-content so long as you have not avowed it. This is the row most easily counterfeited in the whole field of occurrence.

And the solitary subject's A plus F stands entire. In a universe with no second subject, recognition has no object and the S column stays empty forever, while A plus F goes through exactly as before, and that one bearer has its own value-content just the same.
